title: The Southern Advance
subtitle: Kharkov, Crimea, and the continuing German offensive in Ukraine.
author: Robert M. Dobo
summary: Kharkov falls as industrial evacuation preserves resources, Sixth Army brings its occupation policies east and Romanian forces massacre Jews at Odessa.
body:
A southern war with its own clock

On 24 October 1941, German Sixth Army took Kharkov, the industrial and railway city in eastern Ukraine. The event occurred while Moscow remained under an emergency regime and Army Group Centre struggled along its own approach roads. Neither development was a subordinate footnote to the other. Army Group South, commanded by Gerd von Rundstedt, pursued a cluster of objectives: Kharkov, the Donets industrial basin, the route towards Rostov and the entrance to the Crimea. Its armies did not move at the same speed or along a single axis. The capture of Kharkov was a clear change of control on this date, but it did not mean that the entire Soviet southern front collapsed or that Germany had gained the city's evacuated machinery.[1][2][3]

The preceding chapter examined the Soviet government's attempt to keep Moscow governable. Kharkov posed another kind of survival question: how to preserve military production when a manufacturing centre lay on the route of an invading army. The German aim was not merely a place name on a map. Kharkov had factories, skilled workers and rail connections that could support Soviet armies; taking it might disrupt their production and communications. The Soviet response combined delaying combat with removal of industrial equipment. Those efforts could succeed in part even if the city was lost. Conversely, a train moving a factory east did not instantly create a replacement factory at the destination. A dated military narrative has to track both the urban battle and the longer movement of productive capacity.[4][3]

The southern campaign placed its own demands on Soviet resources. Sixth Army's advance on Kharkov threatened an industrial centre and the railways through which evacuation and reinforcement passed. Seventeenth Army moved towards the Donets Basin, First Panzer Army towards the lower Don, and Eleventh Army fought for entry into Crimea. Soviet commanders had to preserve enough force to resist on each axis without repeating the disastrous enclosure at Kiev. The result was a campaign in which withdrawal, demolition, industrial removal and local defence served different purposes. A city could be lost even as some of the military and productive resources needed to continue the war escaped east. [2][5]

From Kiev to Kharkov

The great German victory around Kiev in September had damaged Soviet Southwest Front catastrophically. It also required time to process captives, reorganise German formations and push supply beyond the Dnepr. In the following offensive design, Hitler returned the main concentration of panzer strength to Army Group Centre for Typhoon. Army Group South still had to move east, with Sixth Army towards Kharkov, Seventeenth Army into the Donets region, First Panzer Army farther south towards Rostov, and Eleventh Army contesting the Crimea. The redistribution left the southern theatre with a difficult set of tasks over a broad front rather than an unlimited mobile reserve.[2][3]

Walter von Reichenau commanded Sixth Army on the northern side of this theatre. Hermann Hoth, transferred from Third Panzer Group in October, now commanded Seventeenth Army farther south. Ewald von Kleist's First Panzer Army pursued the lower-Don direction. Their movements had to protect one another's flanks while pursuing different objectives. The infantry armies could not simply match the pace of the mobile formations, and a faster advance by one command could enlarge the area another had to cover. Rundstedt's difficulty was therefore not just deciding which city to attack. It was maintaining enough connection between his armies to support the advance across a widening front. [3][5]

The Soviet response was no longer the defence of Kiev's giant salient. Semyon Timoshenko had been given overall responsibility for the southwestern theatre after the earlier disaster, and the fronts had to decide which cities could be defended, which forces should withdraw and what equipment could be sent east. The units near Kharkov faced the German Sixth Army while the larger Soviet command watched threats in the Donets Basin and Crimea. The possibility of another vast pocket made holding ground at any cost especially dangerous. Kirchubel describes Soviet withdrawal decisions designed to avoid a new encirclement at Kharkov. That does not make the defence token or the loss insignificant; it shows that preservation of forces and industrial equipment could be a different objective from permanent possession of the city.[2][3]

The difference between a mobile and a sustained advance was visible behind the front. German troops crossing the Dnepr could not feed an army from the far bank without bridges, pontoon routes or converted rail lines. Kirchubel describes damaged bridges, ice threatening temporary crossings and railway-gauge work that did not yet put European-gauge service close enough to every forward unit. These constraints did not halt all movement on 24 October. They explain why a command could take a major city yet struggle to send adequate supply to the formations needed for the next objective. This southern logistics problem paralleled that outside Moscow but played out through the Dnepr crossings and Ukraine's long eastward transport corridors.[3][5]

Kharkov on the twenty-fourth

Sixth Army took Kharkov on 24 October after approaching the city from the west and north. Its capture removed a major urban and railway centre from Soviet control, but the defending forces had withdrawn rather than accept another vast encirclement. The result differed from Kiev. Germany gained an important position, while the Soviet command retained forces and some evacuated productive resources with which to continue the war. Neither outcome made the fighting costless. The loss exposed the remaining population to occupation and deprived the Soviet state of a functioning industrial city, even where equipment had been taken away before the Germans arrived. [1][2][3]

Kharkov, now Kharkiv, contained a substantial Jewish community as well as its factories and railways. The Encyclopaedia Judaica account records that many Jews left before German occupation. It does not establish a common reason why others remained, and their circumstances should not be replaced by assumptions about ignorance, confidence or choice. Those still in the city now faced authorities whose persecution of Jews was already established elsewhere. The mass killings associated with Kharkov's later occupation had not all occurred on 24 October. The immediate change was that escape and ordinary life would now be governed by the power of the occupiers. [1]

Control of a city also meant control of a rail junction. Railways out of Kharkov could potentially serve German operations towards the Donets region and Soviet withdrawal routes farther east. But a captured station was not automatically a working German supply hub. Tracks might be damaged, rolling stock removed and gauge conversion unfinished; fuel had to reach the station before trucks could distribute it to troops. The Soviet defenders and evacuation authorities tried to deny Germany the immediate use of productive machinery, while the Germans needed the roads and rail lines to support their continued advance. The difference between possessing infrastructure and operating it is central to understanding the day.[4][3]

For Soviet soldiers defending the approaches, a withdrawal could be both a defeat and a means of preserving combat power. After the September destruction near Kiev, the loss of a further army in another enclosure would be especially dangerous. A unit ordered to delay German entry needed to judge how long a position could be held before its retreat road closed. Such judgments varied by unit and are not reducible to one heroic or cowardly decision. The record supports an organised Soviet effort to remove equipment and to avoid a second vast trap. It does not support a precise claim that every soldier defending Kharkov escaped, nor that every industrial asset was saved. The city fell; the Soviet ability to continue fighting and producing depended on what had moved away before it did.[3][4]

A city and its machinery

Kharkov's capture did not mean Germany acquired an operating tank-production centre on 24 October. Soviet authorities had moved industrial assets east, but Harrison's later account shows that recommissioning could take weeks or far longer. The military value of a factory depended on people, power, parts and transport as much as on its building.[4][1]

Industry as a moving target

The Kharkiv Historical Museum dates the evacuation of the tractor factory from 18 September to 20 October. Its account records the removal of 3,745 of the 3,851 large machine tools and other pieces of equipment designated for evacuation. The figures concern this enterprise's selected equipment, not all industry in Kharkov. They show how much could be removed before the city's capture, while also revealing that evacuation began more than a month before that date. Equipment and workers went through Stalingrad and later to Rubtsovsk, helping to establish the Altai tractor plant. The museum dates that plant's first tractor to August 1942. Industrial preservation was a sequence of departures, installations and delayed production, rather than an intact factory reappearing instantly in the east. [6]

An evacuated plant was more than a set of machine tools. Skilled workers knew tolerances, repair techniques and the informal solutions that let production continue when supplies were scarce. They needed housing and food at the destination. A Soviet army could have a nominal requirement for new tanks, but a dismantled and travelling factory could not meet it that week. Harrison's broader argument is that evacuation preserved the possibility of military survival while imposing major strains on transport, power and consumption in the interior. The RUDN Journal of Russian History's published abstract likewise emphasises the difficulties and losses of armour-industry evacuation rather than treating removal as a frictionless achievement. Those later assessments explain the stakes of the Kharkov decision without erasing the disruption experienced by workers.[4][7]

This example also requires care about industrial identities. Kharkov's tractor works and its tank-producing enterprises should not be treated as interchangeable simply because both belonged to the city's war economy. Harrison's general account uses a rapid resumption example associated with Kharkov; the museum's plant-specific history gives a different sequence for the tractor enterprise and its move to Altai. The secure conclusion is the scale and importance of industrial removal, not a universal restart interval. Some assets could contribute again quickly; others required much longer. For the army waiting for weapons, the decisive measure was usable output, while the state's evacuation policy was also preserving resources for future campaigns. [4][6]

Moving equipment also moved skilled labour and responsibility for supporting it. The receiving regions had to provide accommodation, food, power and transport for enterprises that had not been part of their earlier capacity. Harrison describes the resulting imbalances: preserving arms production could intensify shortages in the civilian economy that sustained it. The factory's departure therefore redistributed the burden of the invasion far beyond the front. Kharkov lost workplaces and machinery; eastern communities acquired additional demands under wartime scarcity. This was a major achievement of mobilisation, but its success depended on people enduring disruption and building workable production arrangements in circumstances for which the destinations were poorly prepared. [6][4]

Other southern directions

Kharkov was only one point in Army Group South's operations. Farther south, Seventeenth Army pressed through the Donets region against Soviet defenders whose retreat and local resistance made German progress uneven. First Panzer Army moved towards Taganrog and Rostov, with its mobile formations dependent on long supply corridors and flank protection. The U.S. Army's planning study places First Panzer Army in the Taganrog area by 20 October and describes stronger resistance and mud affecting Seventeenth and Sixth Armies. It also records attrition in Sixth Army. These broad placements support the picture of a wide offensive with different rates of advance; they do not identify every village or crossing held at noon on the twenty-fourth.[5][3]

The coal and industrial districts of the Donets Basin had strategic significance because the Soviet war effort needed fuel, metals, machinery and rail links. German command could threaten those resources by occupying ground, but the same questions of evacuation and operating capacity applied. Soviet troops and local workers had to decide what could be removed, defended or denied. Kirchubel describes worker militia joining regular Soviet forces in the region and German infantry employing local wagons when its own mobility lagged. Those details matter because they reveal a campaign that cannot be explained by tank arrows alone. Soldiers travelled and fought in a landscape worked by civilians whose mines, railways and factories were objectives of the war.[3][4]

In Crimea, Eleventh Army under Erich von Manstein faced a succession of narrow defensive positions. The October battle was for the Ishun positions south of Perekop, rather than the first entry into the Perekop defences. The offensive there began on 18 October. Lakes and constricted passages reduced the space available for manoeuvre, while Soviet troops evacuated from Odessa helped reinforce the defenders. On 24 October the decisive penetration into the peninsula had not yet been completed. Sevastopol remained Soviet-held, and the later division of Soviet forces between the western fortress and the Kerch direction was still ahead. Treating all of Crimea as German territory would erase an active battle whose outcome mattered to both the Black Sea Fleet and the civilian population.[3][5]

At Odessa, now Odesa, Romanian occupation had already turned into mass murder. After an explosion at the Romanian headquarters on 22 October, Ion Antonescu ordered retaliation against Jews and Communists; the Holocaust Museum notes that responsibility for the explosion remains unclear. Romanian authorities hanged thousands, mostly Jews, on 22–23 October. On the twenty-fourth they moved detained Jews to Dalnyk, where Romanian troops shot people and confined others in buildings attacked with gunfire and fire. The killings continued on 25 October, when explosives were also used. The estimate of roughly 20,000 victims at Dalnyk concerns the massacre as a whole, not deaths on 24 October alone. [8]

German perpetrators also operated in the city. Sonderkommando 11b of Einsatzgruppe D shot an unknown number of Jews from the Fontans'ka Street prison on 23 October. Naming that unit clarifies its involvement without transferring responsibility for the Romanian massacres to an anonymous Axis collective. The victims were selected and killed by identifiable authorities; the claim of retaliation did not establish their responsibility for the explosion. [8]

A city still defended

Sevastopol remained Soviet-held on 24 October. German Eleventh Army was still fighting to penetrate the Crimea; the later encirclement of the fortress cannot be backdated to this entry. Odessa, meanwhile, was under Romanian occupation, and its late-October massacres have a distinct authority and chronology.[5][8]

The army that occupied Kharkov

Reichenau had already instructed Sixth Army on how to understand its war in the east. His order of 10 October demanded ideological participation from soldiers and endorsed antisemitic violence. It treated Jews as the instigators of resistance and condemned what it called misplaced humanity towards civilians and prisoners. Specifically, it prohibited feeding local people and prisoners not working for the Wehrmacht from troop kitchens or giving them bread, even from captured stocks. The order also demanded collective punishment of men deemed able to prevent or report attacks. These instructions placed deprivation and persecution within the commanding general's conception of military duty. [9]

Rundstedt circulated the order on 12 October, declared agreement with it and invited subordinate commands to issue comparable instructions adapted to local circumstances. This establishes endorsement and dissemination at army-group level; it does not by itself document every subsequent act in Kharkov. It does refute an account in which the regular army merely captured the city and left ideological violence to other institutions. [9]

The order's treatment of food connected military supply to the persecution of people under German control. Reichenau presented provisions as resources reserved for the invading force and condemned soldiers who shared them with excluded civilians or prisoners. That was a policy choice about entitlement, not a neutral description of shortage. The invading army faced real transport difficulties, but those difficulties cannot explain away instructions to deny help on racial, political and utilitarian grounds. In occupied Kharkov, the population's vulnerability was sharpened by the removal and destruction of industrial resources before capture. The army entering the city brought its own discriminatory rules about who could receive its support. [9][6]

Soviet demolition and evacuation must also be assessed through their purposes and consequences. Removing machines denied them to Germany and preserved future Soviet production. Destroying assets that could not be moved could deny their use to the invader, while leaving the remaining population with fewer resources. Neither the military rationale nor the civilian consequences should disappear from the account. Harrison's analysis locates these decisions within an emergency struggle to preserve the state and its war economy. The people left in the lost territory did not share equally in the protection that evacuation offered to equipment and selected personnel. Occupation began in communities already disrupted by the retreat. [4][6]

The Soviet side made a converse calculation. A withdrawal from one threatened city could shorten the front and spare formations for another defence, but it meant abandoning residents and land to the occupier. Moving factory equipment could preserve long-term production while consuming trains needed for soldiers and food. Holding Ishun and Sevastopol could keep a Black Sea base and deny Germany a peninsula even as other ground in Ukraine was lost. None of these choices was costless, and there was no single headquarters report that could make them all work. The war in eastern Ukraine was consequently neither pure retreat nor pure German breakthrough. It was a contest over how much combat power and industrial capacity each state could carry into the next month.[2][4][5]

There was also a less familiar item on German staff desks on this exact date. The postwar U.S. Army planning study records an exploratory 24 October discussion of a future Caucasus offensive, including oil fields and routes towards Iran. This was planning for a later campaign, not evidence that German troops were already advancing into the Caucasus or that Hitler had approved every step of the staff concept. Its importance to this chapter is limited but real: even as Kharkov fell and Army Group South struggled to sustain its present movement, planners looked beyond Rostov to objectives whose distance and logistical demands would be greater. The gap between staff possibility and operational means was growing. Readers should not mistake a meeting about what might be attempted for a field order executed on 24 October.[5]

German objectives farther east did not remedy these immediate constraints. The Caucasus oil fields mattered to the strategic imagination of the campaign, but they remained beyond the army's possession. Sixth Army's arrival in Kharkov did not deliver fuel from the Caucasus to an army group still dependent on long western supply routes. The distinction was consequential for operational decisions. Commanders were being urged towards resources whose capture might help sustain a future war, while the attempt to reach them consumed the men, vehicles and provisions available in the present. Success in eastern Ukraine enlarged Germany's commitments before it could deliver the economic transformation the leadership expected. [5][3]

Why the advances did not settle the war

The German capture of Kharkov was an important success. It took a major Soviet city, widened German control in eastern Ukraine and threatened further movement along transport lines. Yet success at one node did not supply every army group or remove Soviet resistance elsewhere. Army Group Centre's attack towards Moscow still depended on roads and formations in its own theatre. Army Group South's leaders still had to decide whether their remaining mobility should be spent on the Donets, the lower Don or support of infantry at Kharkov. Those choices had consequences for flank protection and supply. Kirchubel records disagreements over whether Seventeenth Army should help Sixth Army take Kharkov or continue its own advance. The eventual city capture did not erase the opportunity cost of those debates.[3][2]

The Soviet response preserved part of the capacity the German advance was intended to destroy. Withdrawal prevented a repetition of the great Kiev enclosure at Kharkov, and industrial evacuation removed important assets before occupation. In Crimea, defenders continued to contest entry into the peninsula and protect Sevastopol. These were different achievements, and none reversed the loss of eastern Ukrainian cities. Together they explain why the fall of Kharkov did not settle the southern campaign. The Soviet command still had forces in the field, the state still possessed productive resources farther east, and the occupiers had acquired a city whose population now faced their rule. [3][4][5]

The later occupation would bring hostage-taking, persecution and the mass murder of Kharkov's Jews. Those events belong to their own dates; the city's capture should not absorb them into one undifferentiated day of violence. On 24 October the immediate change was nevertheless profound. A population that had lived under Soviet authority now came under a German army whose commander had explicitly connected military duty with antisemitism and discriminatory deprivation. Reichenau's order did not make every later act inevitable in its particular form. It established the command policy with which the occupiers entered the city and the authority under which soldiers and administrators would act. [1][9]

Kharkov's fall altered the southern war without ending it. Sixth Army had captured an industrial and transport centre; Soviet evacuation had preserved equipment and workers at the price of immediate disruption; the German advance towards the Don and the battle for Crimea continued. For those remaining in Kharkov, the decisive fact was the arrival of an occupying power whose policies threatened their lives and livelihoods. The southern campaign therefore widened both Germany's territorial gains and the demands placed upon its forces. It also showed how a defeated state could continue resisting after losing a city, while the city's inhabitants bore consequences that military accounts of withdrawal could easily overlook. [1][5][4]

sourceMethod: Numbered notes link claims to the consulted passages. The Kharkiv museum’s plant history distinguishes the tractor works from general accounts of tank production. Reichenau’s order and Rundstedt’s covering letter were read in German transcription and paraphrased. The Holocaust Museum supplies the revised Odessa chronology. Kirchubel was consulted through a secondary-hosted chapter transcription; no original page facsimile was available. This is a local prose revision; maps and their separately stored Study Context passages have not been revised.
